title: Gold prices crash  ₹22,000 in a month: Is this the right time to buy to make profits when prices go up? Experts' advice | Stock Market News
text:
Gold prices have corrected sharply over the past month, with MCX gold futures falling by nearly ₹22,000 per 10 grams from around ₹1.43 lakh to ₹1.22 lakh. The decline has brought some relief to consumers preparing for the wedding season, but it has also raised a key question: Is this an opportunity to buy gold at lower levels, or could prices fall further?

The correction has been driven by expectations of another US Federal Reserve rate hike, persistent inflation concerns, elevated US bond yields, a stronger dollar and profit-booking after gold's substantial rally earlier this year. A stronger Indian rupee has added to the pressure on domestic gold prices.

MCX gold is down around 9% year-to-date from approximately ₹1.34 lakh per 10 grams at the end of 2025. It touched a low of ₹1,17,906 per 10 grams on 25 November, marking a decline of around 17% from its level a month earlier and nearly 12% from the start of the year.

On Thursday, 26 November, MCX gold opened with a modest gap-up near ₹1,22,740 per 10 grams and was trading around ₹1,22,580, up approximately 1.2%. The metal was holding above the ₹1,21,000– ₹1,21,700 support zone.

Gold's recovery, however, has been more muted than silver's. MCX gold gained around 1.2%, compared with a 3.2% advance in silver, as the latter staged a stronger rebound following its deeper correction.

With gold prices down sharply and wedding-related demand picking up, experts see the correction as an opportunity for physical buyers. However, they caution against investing the entire amount at once, given the possibility of further volatility and downside risks.

Gaurav Arora, Head of Research at SAHI, said the correction has been driven by expectations of another US Federal Reserve rate hike and persistent inflation in the US. He identified ₹1,17,900 per 10 grams as a key support level and said a fall below ₹1 lakh per 10 grams on MCX appeared unlikely, as it would require a further 18% decline in international gold prices.

Arora said the current correction could offer a buying opportunity for wedding-season consumers, but recommended purchasing in portions because the broader trend remains weak.

Vandana Bharti, Head of Commodity Research at SMC Global Securities, said the nearly ₹22,000 decline from last month's levels has created an attractive opportunity for buyers, particularly those with wedding-related requirements.

She expects MCX gold to find strong support in the ₹1,17,000– ₹1,15,000 per 10 grams zone, from where a rebound is likely. Bharti said a fall below ₹1 lakh per 10 grams appears unlikely under the current outlook, although global economic developments, movements in the dollar and bond yields, and fund flows will remain important factors to watch.

For consumers who need gold for weddings and other personal requirements, she recommended staggered purchases rather than waiting for significantly lower prices. She also cautioned investors and traders against taking aggressive positions in gold derivatives while volatility remains exceptionally high. Physical buyers, she said, can consider gradual accumulation.

Kaveri More, Commodity Technical Analyst at Choice Broking, said the sharp correction has created an attractive buying opportunity for wedding-season buyers, but advised them to purchase in stages rather than commit their entire budget at current levels.

More attributed the decline of nearly ₹22,000 per 10 grams from October levels to global weakness and appreciation in the Indian rupee. She cited rising expectations of a US Federal Reserve rate hike in December, elevated US bond yields, a stronger dollar and profit-booking following gold's substantial rally earlier this year as key reasons behind the correction.

She added that the recent improvement in the rupee had amplified the decline in domestic gold prices, while lower prices and the wedding season could support physical jewellery demand.

From a technical perspective, More said MCX gold futures were trading around ₹1,23,270 per 10 grams on 26 November. She placed immediate support in the ₹1,21,000– ₹1,19,700 per 10 grams range. A sustained break below this zone, she said, could extend the correction towards ₹1,17,000– ₹1,15,000 per 10 grams.

However, she does not expect MCX gold to fall below ₹1 lakh per 10 grams in the near term. Such a move would require a much deeper correction in international bullion prices, accompanied by a persistently stronger dollar and higher US yields.

More recommended that wedding buyers consider purchasing gold in two to three tranches, keeping some funds aside to benefit from any further decline instead of waiting entirely for the ₹1 lakh level.

Jigar Trivedi, Senior Research Analyst at IndusInd Securities, said gold's near-term outlook remains cautious despite the sharp correction in domestic prices. While lower prices have improved affordability for Indian consumers ahead of the wedding season, he cautioned that it may be premature to conclude that the market has established a durable bottom.

Trivedi said international bullion prices remain sensitive to US Federal Reserve policy expectations, movements in the dollar and Treasury yields, as well as geopolitical developments. On the domestic front, seasonal jewellery demand and continued investment interest could provide some support, but physical demand alone may not be enough to reverse the trend if global prices remain under pressure.

He said the possibility of MCX gold slipping below ₹1,10,000 per 10 grams cannot be ruled out, although such a move would require another substantial correction from current levels. A sustained rise in the dollar, higher bond yields and further investor liquidation could increase downside risks.

On the other hand, softer US yields, central-bank purchases and renewed safe-haven demand could trigger a recovery, Trivedi said.

For wedding-season buyers, he recommended a staggered purchasing strategy rather than waiting for a specific price target. Investor
